title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name and where you're from, ask how someone is, and use the verb "to be", which always comes at the end of the sentence.
bekal: greet people with *kaixo*, *egun on*, *arratsalde on*, and *gabon*, each at the right time
say your own name with *nola duzu izena* and answer the question
use *naiz / zara / da* to say "I am / you are / he or she is ..."

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Lehen eguna Bilbon
dialogs.intro: First day in Bilbo. Budi has just walked out of Loiu airport and meets Ainhoa, a staff member from the euskaltegi (Basque language school) who has come to pick him up.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Kaixo! Ongi etorri Bilbora. Ni Ainhoa naiz.
lines.id: Hello! Welcome to Bilbo. I'm Ainhoa.
lines.literal: hello! well come Bilbo-to. I Ainhoa am.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kaixo, Ainhoa. Ni Budi naiz. Pozten naiz.
lines.id: Hello, Ainhoa. I'm Budi. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: hello, Ainhoa. I Budi am. glad am.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: How are you? Are you tired?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ondo, eskerrik asko. Pixka bat nekatuta. Eta zu?
lines.id: Fine, thank you. A bit tired. And you?
lines.literal: fine, thanks many. little one tired. and you?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: Very well. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: That's so far! Do you speak Basque?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pixka bat. Euskara ikasten ari naiz.
lines.literal: little one. Basque learning busy am.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Benetan? Ni ikaslea naiz, eta sukaldaria ere bai.
lines.id: Really? I'm a student, and a cook too.
lines.literal: truly? I student-the am, and cook-the also yes.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Ederra! Tira, goazen. Kotxea hemen dago.
lines.id: Lovely! Right, let's go. The car is here.
lines.literal: beautiful-the! well, let's-go. car-the here is(located).

notes: **Kaixo works any time, but there's often a better fit.** *Kaixo* is a "hello" that is safe with anyone at any hour. But Basques more often greet by time of day: *egun on* in the morning, *arratsalde on* from midday to evening, *gabon* at night. Among friends you'll also hear *aupa!* a lot — roughly a friendly "hey!".

**Zer moduz? calls for a short answer.** Literally "in what way?". The answer is nearly always one word: *ondo* (fine), *oso ondo* (very well), *hala-hola* (so-so), *nekatuta* (tired). A long answer sounds like you're complaining — just like "how are you?" in English.

**"To be" can't be left out — and it goes last.** As in English, *ni ikaslea* ("I student") isn't a sentence yet; it needs *naiz*. But look where it goes: **at the very end**, after everything else — "I student am". That pattern will come back throughout the course.

**Two ways to say where you're from.** For countries and peoples, use *-ar/-tar*: *indonesiarra* (Indonesian), *japoniarra*, *euskalduna* (a Basque, literally "one who has euskara"). For cities, use *-ko/-go*: *Jakartakoa*, *Bilbokoa*, *Donostiakoa*. When in doubt, *-ko* almost always works: *Indonesiakoa naiz* is also correct.

blocks.text: These twelve phrases aren't grammar material — they're your emergency kit. Memorize them whole now; understand how they're built later.

blocks.text: *Ez horregatik* literally means "not because of that" — the standard reply to thanks, and no stranger than "don't mention it" if you think about it too hard. Another one that's just as common: *ez da ezer* ("it's nothing").

blocks.title: One sentence that changes your time in Euskal Herria
items: *Euskara ikasten ari naiz. Euskaraz hitz egin dezakegu?* — "I'm learning Basque. Can we speak euskara?"

Almost every Basque speaker is also fluent in Spanish or French, so they'll switch automatically the moment they hear a foreign accent. The sentence above stops that switch — and it's almost always met with a smile, because outsiders who learn their language are still rare.

blocks.text: Look at the order: the time first, then *on* ("good"). From *egun* (day) → *egun on*, all these greetings are literally short wishes: "day good". Basque puts adjectives **after** the noun, and these greetings are your first example.
*Arte* means "until", and it stands **after** the word it goes with: *gero arte* = "later until". This holds for every word of place and time in Basque — they all come afterwards, never in front.

sections.title: Naiz, zara, da — your first verb

blocks.text: *Izan* means "to be". It's the most important verb in the language, and its forms have to be learned whole — there's no pattern, just like English "am/is/are".

The pronoun itself can be dropped, because the verb form already shows who's meant: *Budi naiz* already means "I'm Budi". Native speakers use *ni*, *zu*, and the rest only for emphasis — "**I'm** the teacher, not her".
Negating: ez in front, and the auxiliary comes with it
To negate, put *ez* in front of the auxiliary — and the auxiliary jumps forward with it, leaving its place at the end of the sentence.

blocks.title: Careful: izan and egon are not the same
items: *Izan* (naiz, zara, da) is for **identity**: who you are, where you're from, your job. *Ni ikaslea naiz.*
*Egon* (nago, zaude, dago) is for **temporary states and location**: where you are, how you're feeling. *Bilbon nago. Nekatuta nago.*

English speakers tend to use *naiz* for both, because English has just one "to be". Quick rule: if it could change by tomorrow, use *egon*. Spanish makes exactly the same split (*ser* and *estar*) — if you've studied Spanish, you already know the feeling.
Unit 11 covers *egon* fully. For now, just memorize two sentences: *Nekatuta nago* and *Bilbon nago*.
